title: Painted sakhis
hook: sakhis became paintings, murals and later posters in Sikh homes
tomorrow: Telling a sakhi to a child

segments.voice: Yesterday, sakhi: the details move between tellings, but the lesson stays. Today, the sakhis leave the page.

In a living room in Birmingham, or Fresno, or Ludhiana, there's a framed picture above the sofa. An old man with a white beard sits under a tree. On one side, a younger man holds a stringed instrument. On the other, a man waves a whisk over him. A child in that house has looked at it every day since before she could read. Ask her who they are, and she'll tell you. Nobody sat her down for a lesson. The wall did it.
screen: `A PICTURE ABOVE THE SOFA.` → `AN OLD MAN UNDER A TREE.` → `THE WALL TAUGHT HER.`

segments.voice: On day seven hundred twenty-six we met B40, a book with a painting beside each sakhi. A book sits on a shelf, and someone has to open it. Today the pictures leave the book. Sakhis went up on walls: murals painted inside gurdwaras and old houses, showing Nanak on the road, at the river, with the yogis on the mountain. Later came printed pictures, posters and calendars, cheap enough to hang in any home. That changes how a picture teaches. A page is seen when you sit down to read it. A wall is seen over and over without trying: on the way to breakfast, in the middle of an argument, on a sick day on the sofa. The girl in that living room never had a lesson. She had years of passing by. Look closer at her picture. The man with the whisk is Bhai Bala, the companion from the Bala tellings, the one historians still discuss. A print has no footnotes. It quietly carries one telling's choices into the house, and its faces are each artist's own imagining. So yesterday's habit works on walls too: ask what the picture knows, and which telling it comes from. Sikh teachers add a caution. A picture is a reminder of a story, not something to bow to. In the gurdwara, the bow goes to the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. The picture points; it doesn't receive.
screen: `FROM SHELF TO WALL.` · `SEEN EVERY DAY WITHOUT TRYING.` · `THE PICTURE CARRIES A TELLING.` · `A REMINDER, NOT AN OBJECT OF WORSHIP.` · then, large: `PICTURES TEACH.`

segments.voice: Look at a picture near you, a family photo, a print, a child's drawing on the fridge, or your phone's lock screen if the walls are bare. Ask what moment someone chose to keep, and what it teaches anyone who passes it every day. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath.
Painted sakhis. Stories of the Gurus carried in pictures: on book pages, on walls, and in printed pictures in homes.
Your line: pictures teach. A wall can teach without a word. Day seven hundred forty-four.
